after: ## The assumptions and what they mean in practice
alt: A table of three rows labels input, process and output: Andrade (telephone message, attention and memory, names recalled), Baron-Cohen et al. (photograph of eyes, inferring a mental state, chosen word) and Pozzulo et al. (target face, encoding and recognition, line-up decision). A note links each study to an assumption.
caption: Every study fits the same input, process, output route.

alt: Forty probably bored participants listened to a dull telephone message and wrote down party guests' names. Half shaded printed shapes while listening. In a surprise recall test the doodling group recalled about 29% more than the control group and were more accurate on the monitoring task.
caption: Shading shapes during a dull message raised recall by about 29%.

after: ## Baron-Cohen et al. (2001): the eyes test
alt: A table compares the original Eyes test (two answer choices, too few items, a ceiling effect) with the revised version (four words, 36 photographs, a glossary, better separation of people). A schematic item shows a photograph of the eye region with one target word and three foils.
caption: Four choices and 36 items reduced guessing and the ceiling effect.

after: ## Baron-Cohen et al. (2001): the eyes test
alt: Two parts of the design: a quasi-experiment comparing four adult groups, and a correlation between Eyes test and Autism Spectrum Quotient scores. The autism group scored significantly lower, and an illustrative scatter shows that higher AQ scores went with lower Eyes test scores.
caption: More autistic traits went with lower Eyes test scores.

alt: Two line-ups of four people. In the target-present line-up the culprit (gold) is included; in the target-absent line-up the culprit is missing, so choosing anyone is a false positive. Children made more false positive responses than adults in target-absent line-ups.
caption: In a target-absent line-up any choice is a false positive, and children made more.
